A Day in the Life of Kaamadhenu
To truly appreciate what Project Kaamadhenu represents, it helps to imagine a single day in the life of the Goshala — from the pre-dawn stillness of the Ashram to the quiet of evening.
Before Dawn: The Day Begins

Long before the sun rises over the Ashram, the Goshala staff are already at work. Cattle, like all large animals, have deep physiological rhythms that demand early attention. The first task of the day is to check on every animal — to walk through the shelters in the soft glow of early morning light, noticing which animals seem well and which might need attention, checking that water troughs are full and that the cooling systems are functioning.

The milking cows are attended to in the early morning hours. Milking is done gently, by hand or with appropriate equipment, always ensuring that calves have received their share first. There is no industrial urgency here, no pressure to maximise extraction at the expense of the animal's comfort. The milk that the Goshala takes is what the cow offers freely after her calf is satisfied.
Morning: Feeding and Tending

As the sun rises and the Ashram comes to life with the sounds of morning prayers and devotional music, the Goshala is filled with the activity of feeding. Green fodder, freshly cut from the organic grass fields, is distributed. Concentrated feed — grains, pulses, mineral supplements — is prepared and apportioned according to each animal's needs. The calves receive their morning meal with particular attention, their young bodies requiring precise nutrition for healthy development.

Staff observe each animal as they eat. A cow who eats eagerly is a healthy cow. A cow who stands apart from the feed, or who eats less than usual, may be signalling an oncoming illness or a discomfort that needs investigation. This kind of daily, attentive observation is one of the most important forms of veterinary care — catching problems early, before they become serious.
Midday: Shelter and Rest

The South Indian sun at midday is intense, and the Goshala's shelters come into their most important function during these hours. Animals rest in the shade, the fans creating a gentle air movement that prevents heat stress. The shelters hum quietly with the sound of breathing, of occasional gentle lowing, of calves settling near their mothers.

This is also the time for maintenance work — cleaning shelters, managing the waste collection systems, tending to the grass fields, repairing any infrastructure that needs attention. The work of a Goshala is never finished; it simply shifts from one task to the next, sustained by the quiet dedication of people who understand that they are participating in something sacred.
Evening: Gratitude and Rest

As the heat of the day eases and the Ashram moves into its evening rhythm of prayers and communal gatherings, the Goshala settles into its end-of-day routine. The animals are checked again. The evening feeding is completed. Fresh water is provided. Any animal showing signs of distress or illness receives attention from the Goshala's veterinary staff.

In the Hindu devotional tradition, the cow is associated with the auspicious hours of dawn and dusk — the sandhya kala, the transitional moments between day and night. Many Ashram residents come to the Goshala at these hours to simply be in the presence of the animals, to offer them a gentle touch, to sit in the warm, grassy-smelling air of the shelters and feel the particular quality of peace that comes from being near large, gentle creatures living contentedly.

This peace is not incidental. It is part of what the Goshala offers to the human community as much as to the animals themselves. The cows of Kaamadhenu give milk and dung and their gentle presence. They receive food and shelter and care. And in this exchange — this ancient, reciprocal relationship between human and cow — something that is difficult to name but unmistakable to experience takes place. A healing. A reminder of what life can be when it is lived in genuine relationship with other beings.
The Challenges: Honesty About What It Takes

A document that speaks only of beauty and achievement would be incomplete. The reality of caring for 300+ large animals is demanding in ways that are important to understand — both because honesty demands it, and because understanding the challenges is essential to understanding the need for support.
The Financial Demands

Maintaining the Goshala at the standard that Amma and the Ashram have set is expensive. The costs are substantial and continuous. Feed for 300+ animals, including the high-quality concentrated rations and the organic green fodder that requires field maintenance and irrigation, represents a significant daily expense. Veterinary care — vaccinations, deworming, treatment of illnesses and injuries, obstetric care for pregnant cows — is a regular and non-negotiable cost.

Infrastructure maintenance — keeping the shelters in good repair, maintaining the cooling and ventilation systems, servicing the water supply, managing the waste systems — requires ongoing investment. Staff salaries must be paid. The planned biogas infrastructure requires initial capital investment before it begins to generate savings.

There is no month in which the Goshala does not need financial support. Unlike a project with a clear endpoint — a building to be constructed, an event to be organised — a Goshala is a perpetual commitment. Every day, every week, every year, the animals need feeding, the shelters need maintaining, the staff need to be paid. The generosity that makes Kaamadhenu possible must be as continuous as the care it supports.
The Human Demands

Beyond finance, the Goshala demands human presence. Cows cannot be left unattended. They cannot be fed by timers or managed by remote systems in the way that some forms of automated agriculture attempt. They are living, social beings who require genuine human attention — the attention of people who know them as individuals, who notice when something is wrong, who provide the kind of calm, confident, affectionate handling that keeps large animals settled and cooperative.

Finding, training, and retaining dedicated Goshala staff is itself a significant ongoing task. The work is physically demanding and requires a particular combination of knowledge, physical capability, and genuine love for the animals. The Ashram relies on a core team of experienced caregivers and supplements them with the labour of devoted volunteers — people who come from the local community, from among Ashram residents, and sometimes from further afield, drawn by the opportunity to serve in what they understand as a form of sacred practice.
How You Can Be Part of This Sacred Mission

Project Kaamadhenu is not the private project of a single institution. It is an open invitation — to anyone who values the life of an animal, who cares about sustainable living, who wants to support the continuation of a tradition of compassion that is twenty years old and counting — to become part of something important.
Financial Contributions: Every Gift Feeds a Life

The most immediate way to support Kaamadhenu is through financial contribution. Every rupee, every dollar, every euro, every pound that is given goes directly to the care of the animals. There is no bureaucratic layer here, no administrative overhead that absorbs donations before they reach their destination. The Ashram is a lean institution animated by genuine devotion, and contributions translate directly into feed, medicine, and maintenance.

Donors can choose to contribute in a variety of meaningful ways. A one-time gift helps meet an immediate need. A monthly recurring contribution provides the predictable support that allows for long-term planning. A significant donation to capital projects — the biogas infrastructure, the expansion of shelter capacity, the development of additional grass fields — creates lasting improvements to the Goshala's capability.

Some donors find it meaningful to make their gifts in honour of specific occasions: a birthday, a memorial for a loved one, an anniversary, a festival. A gift to the Goshala on the occasion of Gopashtami — the Hindu festival that specifically celebrates the cow — carries particular resonance. So does a gift made during Navratri, the nine-night festival of the Divine Mother, in whose honour the Goshala was ultimately built.
The Meaning of Cow Seva: Spiritual Significance of Giving

In the Hindu understanding, service to the cow — Gousheva or Gau Seva — is among the most meritorious of all acts of charity. Ancient texts speak of the spiritual benefits that accrue to those who feed a cow, who provide shelter for a cow, who contribute to the care of a cow in need. This is not superstition. It is a recognition that the act of caring for a vulnerable, sacred creature — one who cannot advocate for herself, who gives so much and asks only to be treated with kindness — is an act that elevates the giver as surely as it protects the animal.

For devotees of Amma and of the Hindu spiritual tradition, contributing to Kaamadhenu is not merely philanthropy. It is worship. It is a way of expressing in material, practical terms the reverence for life that one holds in one's heart. It is a way of participating in the Ashram's sacred mission even from a distance — of being, in some small but real way, part of the community of care that gathers around these extraordinary animals every single day.
Volunteering: The Gift of Presence

For those who have the opportunity to be physically present at the Ashram, volunteering in the Goshala is one of the most transformative experiences available. There is something that happens when a human being spends time in genuine, attentive service to a large animal — something that cannot be fully described but only experienced.

Goshala volunteers participate in a range of activities depending on their physical capability and experience. Feeding and watering the animals. Cleaning and maintaining the shelters. Assisting with the grass field cultivation. Helping with the management of calves. Simply spending time with the animals — grooming them, sitting with them, offering them the gentle human presence that is itself a form of nourishment.

Many volunteers report that their time in the Goshala is among the most peaceful and grounding experiences they have had. The pace of the work — repetitive, physical, earthy, completely removed from the abstractions of modern life — creates a particular quality of presence. You are not planning or worrying or performing. You are simply here, with this creature, doing this necessary thing. It is, in its way, a form of meditation.

The Ashram welcomes volunteers from all backgrounds, all traditions, all countries. You do not need to be Hindu. You do not need to be a spiritual seeker. You need only to be willing to work, to be gentle with the animals, and to approach the experience with an open heart.
Spreading the Word: The Power of Story

Not everyone can donate financially or volunteer in person. But everyone who is moved by the story of Kaamadhenu can help it reach further by sharing it — with friends, with family, on social media, in conversations. The more people who know that a place like this exists, the more the vision it embodies — of compassion, of sustainability, of sacred animal care — can influence the way people think and act toward cattle everywhere in the world.

If you are an animal welfare advocate, a veterinarian, a farmer exploring sustainable practices, a journalist, a documentary filmmaker, a student of religion or ecology or ethics — the story of Kaamadhenu may be relevant to your work. The Ashram welcomes inquiries from anyone who wishes to learn more, to visit, to collaborate, or to help tell this story to a wider world.
Looking Forward: The Vision for Kaamadhenu 's Future

Twenty years into its journey, Project Kaamadhenu is not resting. It is growing, evolving, and extending its vision in ways that promise to make it an even more significant contributor to the spiritual, ecological, and social landscape of the Ashram and its surrounding community.
Full Energy Self-Sufficiency Through Biogas

The completion and full operationalisation of the biogas programme is among the most immediate priorities. When this system is fully running, the Goshala will achieve a level of energy self-sufficiency that is remarkable for an operation of its scale. The cooking requirements of the Ashram — substantial, given the large community of residents and the thousands of visitors who come for festivals and retreats — will be met by the clean, renewable energy generated from the dung of the Goshala's own animals.

Beyond the practical benefits, the biogas programme will be a powerful symbol and a practical demonstration of a principle that has enormous global relevance: that integrated animal-agricultural systems, managed with care and intelligence, can be not just ecologically neutral but ecologically positive — generating clean energy, enriching soil, and reducing the carbon footprint of human community rather than expanding it.
Model and Inspiration for Others

The Ashram and its leadership are aware that what has been built at Kaamadhenu has significance beyond its own walls. The model — of a large, sustainable, compassionate Goshala integrated with organic agriculture, zero-waste management, and community nourishment — is replicable. Other Ashrams, other communities, other individuals who wish to honour the cow and care for animals can learn from what has been built here.

There is a vision of Kaamadhenu becoming not just a sanctuary but a centre of learning — a place where those interested in traditional cow care, in Ayurvedic uses of cow products, in organic farming, in biogas technology, in the spiritual dimensions of animal care can come to learn, to observe, and to take back knowledge to their own communities and projects.
The Enduring Vision: Dharma in Practice

At the deepest level, the vision for Kaamadhenu 's future is not about any specific programme or infrastructure project. It is about the enduring demonstration, year after year and generation after generation, that dharma — righteous, compassionate, ecologically harmonious living — is not an ideal confined to scripture but a practical reality that can be built, maintained, and handed on.

Amma has begun something extraordinary. The twenty years that have passed since two cows first came to live at the Ashram have proven that the vision is viable, that the commitment is sustainable, that the love is real and lasting. The task now is to ensure that what has been built continues and grows — that the 300+ animals in residence today are followed by generations of animals cared for with the same tenderness, that the sustainable systems developed at Kaamadhenu continue to evolve and improve, and that the story of this place continues to inspire and challenge people all over the world to think differently about how they relate to the animals who share our earth.
A Final Word: The Cow's Gift to Humanity

There is an old Sanskrit saying: Sarve bhavantu sukhinah — may all beings be happy. It is one of the oldest and most universal of human prayers, and it contains within it a recognition that the happiness of all beings is not separate from our own. We are not independent of the creatures around us. We are woven together in a web of interdependence so ancient and so intricate that we have only begun to understand it.

The cow stands at the centre of one of the most important of those webs of interdependence. She has nourished us since the earliest days of human settlement. She has been, in the literal biological sense, a second mother to billions of human beings. She has fertilised the fields that fed us, pulled the ploughs that cultivated our crops, provided the fuel that cooked our food. She has asked nothing in return except to be treated with the basic dignity that any creature who gives so much deserves to receive.

Project Kaamadhenu is, at its heart, an expression of gratitude. Gratitude for what the cow has given. Gratitude expressed not in words but in action — in the daily, unglamorous, deeply loving work of feeding and sheltering and healing and protecting 300+ animals who can never fully know what is being done for them, or why, but who respond to it with the simple, wordless, heartbreaking generosity of their nature: with their milk, with their gentle presence, with the particular peace that comes from being near a creature who is truly, completely, unconditionally cared for.

If you are reading this, and something in this story has moved you — if you have felt, even for a moment, the truth of what is being offered here — then Project Kaamadhenu invites you to be part of it. Give what you can. Come if you are able. Tell the story. And wherever you are in the world, in whatever way you can, honour the life of the cow.

For in doing so, you honour the source of your own nourishment. You honour the earth that holds you. You honour the ancient, sacred covenant between human beings and the animals who have always been our most generous and faithful companions.
"Gaavoh vishvasya maatarah" — The cow is the mother of the world. (Rigveda)
